title: No Rain, No Grain: Why Your Breakfast Cereal Might Get Pricier
summary: Have you ever left a plant without water for too long? It gets all droopy and sad. Now imagine that happening to entire fields of wheat, oats, and vegetables across a whole country. That's exactly what's going on in England and Wales right now. A long, hot drought has turned the ground so dry that farmers are really worried. Tom Bradshaw, the president of the National Farmers' Union (a big group that speaks for farmers), says the crops are doing terribly. "Yields of wheat and oats are very, very poor this year," he explained. That means there's way less grain growing than usual. And it's not just plants. Livestock farmers, who raise cows and sheep, have already had to start using their winter food supplies because the grass won't grow. It's like eating all your emergency snacks in July instead of saving them for December! Over 20 million people are now under hosepipe bans—that means they can't use a hose to water their gardens or wash their cars. Rivers are running low, and vegetable growers are struggling to get enough water for their crops. This makes the veggies more expensive to grow, and there might not be as many in the shops. Bradshaw says we need to think ahead. He wants the government to build more reservoirs (giant lakes that store rainwater) so we don't waste water that flows into the sea in winter. He also thinks farmers should get tax breaks to build their own water storage. "We have taken our food supply for granted for far too long," he warned. So next time you pour milk on your cereal, remember: the weather affects way more than just your plans to go to the park.
why_it_matters: The cereal, bread, and milk you eat every day start on farms that depend on weather—so a dry spell can make your breakfast cost more or even become hard to find.

background_read: Even rainy places like England and Wales can have droughts. In 1976, a famous dry spell caused rivers to shrink and food prices to rise. Scientists say that climate change may bring hotter, drier summers more often. The National Farmers' Union (a group that speaks for over 55,000 farmers) warns that without more water storage, food supplies could be in trouble.
Article_Structure: WHO: Tom Bradshaw, president of the National Farmers' Union.
WHAT: He warned that a severe drought is causing very poor wheat and oat yields and forcing early use of winter animal feed.
WHY: Because the hot, dry weather stops crops and grass from growing, raising food prices and showing the need for more reservoirs and water planning.
